caseNote: 가상 사례 (B2B 마케팅 에이전시 공동창업자, 식자재 도매 유통 공동대표) · 적용 레슨으로 SAL-05-03(여러 쟁점 동시 협상)과 SAL-05-05(전술적 공감)를 함께 사용
insight: 공동창업자의 역할 다툼은 직함 하나를 두고 싸우는 일이 아니다. 직함을 여러 쟁점으로 풀어 맞바꾸고, 그 밑에 깔린 두려움을 말로 짚어 줄 때 풀린다.
misconception: 역할 분담은 누가 더 잘하는지, 지분이 누가 더 많은지로 정하면 끝나는 문제다. 감정은 빼고 논리로만 정리해야 한다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes. 입장이 아닌 이해관계에 집중하고 여러 쟁점을 교환하는 원리
Voss, C. (2016). Never Split the Difference. 전술적 공감과 라벨링(감정 이름 붙이기)
모든 사례와 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 인물, 회사, 상황은 가상입니다. 실제 기업 수치나 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다.
'tactical empathy'와 라벨링 표현('It sounds like…')은 Voss(2016)의 용어입니다. SAL-05-05 본문의 정의·예시 표현과 일치하는지 게시 전 확인하세요.
지분, 의결권, 계약서 작성 등 법률·세무 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 7번 카드에서 '역할을 글로 적어 두라'는 수준으로만 다뤘습니다. 법률 검토 권고 문구가 필요한지 편집 판단이 필요합니다.

cards.title: Two founders, one CEO title
body: Maya and Daniel started a B2B marketing agency two years ago. Now they have twelve staff, a first investor meeting, and a form that asks for one name next to *CEO*.
They've avoided the question for months. Tonight, at a whiteboard, they both want the title.

image.label: Two founders at a whiteboard with one empty CEO box
image.brief: 늦은 저녁 작은 사무실. 화이트보드 가운데 'CEO'라고 적힌 빈 칸 하나, 그 앞에 마커를 든 두 공동창업자가 서로 다른 방향을 보고 서 있음. 따뜻한 조명, 약간 긴장된 분위기. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should they start?
body: Maya brings in most clients. Daniel runs delivery and the finances. Each thinks the title should be theirs.

options.feedback: It ends tonight's fight, but it hides the real questions. Who decides when they disagree on hiring or spending? The deadlock just moves to later.

options.text: List everything "CEO" means to each of them, then trade
options.feedback: This is **many issues at once** at work. One title can't be split, but the powers inside it can. More issues means more room to trade.

options.text: Whoever owns more of the company gets it
options.feedback: Fast and clear, but it decides by ownership, not by what the company needs. The founder who loses may stop pulling their weight.

cards.title: The title was a bundle.
body: They each wrote what being CEO would give them. The lists barely overlapped.
Maya wanted to be the face of the firm: pitching, speaking at events, owning the big client relationships. Daniel wanted final say on hiring and on any spending over $5,000.
Fighting over the word, they looked like rivals. Split into parts, most of what each wanted didn't cost the other much.

image.label: One CEO box split into separate role cards
image.brief: 'CEO' 상자 하나가 여러 장의 카드로 쪼개지는 그림. 카드 라벨: 'Public face', 'Big clients', 'Hiring', 'Spending', 'Tie-breaker'. 일부 카드는 왼쪽 인물 쪽으로, 일부는 오른쪽 인물 쪽으로 이동.

cards.title: Under the position, a fear.
body: One item stayed stuck: the title itself. Daniel wouldn't move.
Maya stopped arguing and said, "It sounds like you're worried that if I'm CEO, people will treat you as the junior partner." Daniel paused. "Yes. Clients already call you first."

That is **tactical empathy**: naming the other person's feeling out loud so they feel understood. It doesn't mean agreeing. It brought the real issue, respect, onto the table, where it could be traded too.

cards.title: "Fine. Take it. I'll just do the work."
body: Imagine Daniel had said this instead, arms crossed. As Maya, what's your next line?

options.feedback: You win the title and lose a partner. A yes given in anger tends to come back as resentment months later.

options.text: "It sounds like this feels like losing, not deciding."
options.feedback: **Tactical empathy** names the feeling behind the words. It invites Daniel to say what he actually needs, which is something you can still give.

options.text: "Let me explain why it's logical for me to be CEO."
options.feedback: Your reasons may be good, but he isn't objecting to the logic. Facts land better once he feels heard.

cards.title: What they wrote down
body: Each gave up what mattered less to them to get what mattered more.
cards.softwareNote: In software startups the fight is often over "product." Split it: who owns the roadmap, who says no to a feature, who talks to key users, who hires engineers. Each piece can go to a different founder.

cards.title: Trades need a tie-breaker and a paper trail.
body: Splitting roles works only if the lines are written down. Memories of a late-night talk drift, and each founder remembers the version that favors them.
Some issues can't be split evenly. If two people each hold half of a decision with no tie-breaker, you've built a deadlock into the company. Decide now who settles which kind of dispute.
And empathy isn't a trick. If you name someone's fear only to steer them, they'll notice, and trust will suffer.

cards.title: Now it's a food distributor.
body: Priya and Tom co-own a wholesale business that supplies restaurants. Both want to run purchasing. Tom says, "Buying is the job that matters. Everything else is admin."

options.text: Priya takes purchasing because she negotiates better prices
options.feedback: Maybe true, but Tom hears "your job is admin." Without a trade or an acknowledgement, he may fight every buying decision.

options.text: First say, "It sounds like you're afraid of being sidelined," then split purchasing by category and trade warehouse and delivery ownership
options.feedback: Both tools at once. **Tactical empathy** surfaces the fear. **Many issues at once** turns one contested job into several that can be traded.
Fair on the surface, but suppliers lose a steady contact and each year starts with a handover. It avoids the trade instead of making one.

cards.title: Don't divide the title. Divide what's inside it.
body: This lesson used two tools. **Many issues at once:** break one contested role into parts and trade them. **Tactical empathy:** name the fear behind a hard position so it can be dealt with.
**Try it today:** write down the five decisions you and your partner or closest colleague argue about most. Next to each, write who should have the final say.
